aliases: Hungerford Bridge and Golden Jubilee Bridges

claims.text: The Golden Jubilee Bridges are actually two stunning cable-stayed pedestrian bridges that flank the older central steel truss railway bridge.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The very first crossing here was a suspension footbridge designed by Isambard Kingdom Brunel that opened in 1845.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: In 1864, the Charing Cross Railway Company completely replaced the old footbridge with a new railway structure designed by Sir John Hawkshaw.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Amazingly, the heavy chains from Brunel's original bridge were saved and famously reused to build Bristol's Clifton Suspension Bridge.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: The original brick pile buttresses from Brunel's very first footbridge are actually still in use today.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: Before the new Golden Jubilee Bridges were built following a 1996 design competition, pedestrians had to use a narrow, dilapidated, and dangerous walkway attached to the railway bridge.
claims.subject: self

claims.text: As an added bonus, the construction of these new pedestrian structures helped protect the vulnerable iron pillars of the old railway bridge from dangerous riverboat impacts.
claims.subject: self
